sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
Ag, Ag-Cu and Cu dendrite catalysts were electrochemically prepared on a Cu foil substrate to investigate their catalytic activity and selectivity for electrochemical CO2 reduction to CO. As the Cu content increased, the morphologies of Ag-Cu dendrite catalysts changed significantly from round to flower-like shapes accompanied by a decrease in branch size of the dendritic structure. A crystallographic study of the Ag-Cu dendrite catalysts demonstrated the formation of Ag and Cu co-deposits, while a compositional characterization confirmed the presence of a Cu-rich surface. Among the synthesized dendrite catalysts, the Ag100 dendrite catalyst achieved the highest CO faradaic efficiency of 64.6 % at a constant potential of -1.7 VSCE in CO2saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte. However, the catalytic activity of Ag57Cu43 dendrite catalyst was 2.2 times higher than that of the Ag100 dendrite catalyst, in terms of Ag mass activity. By controlling the composition of Ag and Cu, direct formation of syn-gas or enhancement in the mass activity to CO production was achievable.
Keywords: electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction; carbon monoxide production; electrodeposition; silver-copper dendrite catalyst

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Carbon dioxide (CO2) gas from industries and vehicles, is a major contributor to the greenhouse effect responsible for bringing about serious global warming [1]. Among various methods to convert CO2 into useful chemicals [2-5], electrochemical CO2 reduction on electrocatalysts facilitates a clean process when combined with external electricity from renewable sources (e.g. sunlight, wind and etc.) [6,7]. There are several reusable forms of carbon produced by the electrochemical CO2 reduction in aqueous electrolytes such as formic acid/formate, methanol, methane and carbon monoxide [6]. Among these, CO is a component of syn-gas which is a useful feedstock for the Fischer-Tropsch process to generate hydrocarbon fuels [8]. Furthermore, unlike other liquid products, the gaseous CO has an advantage: it does not need to be extracted from the electrolyte.
The main challenges in the electrochemical reduction of CO2 are the low energy efficiency and poor selectivity of the process [9]. The electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO is relatively simpler compared to other products primarily because it is a two-electron reduction process: CO2 + 2H + + 2e-→ CO + H2O, E 0 = -0.53 V [9]. Still, a large overpotential is required for this process because CO2 is thermodynamically and chemically stable. Therefore, the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) competes with the electrochemical CO2 reduction in CO2-saturated aqueous electrolytes. Thus, there is an urgent requirement for the development of
4
electrocatalysts, both with robust activity and high selectivity for CO production.
Many studies have been conducted on various metal electrodes for electrochemical CO2 reduction [10-27]. Among them, the noble metal electrocatalysts, such as gold (Au) [13-16] and silver (Ag) [17-20] exhibit high CO selectivity at moderate overpotentials. The catalytic performance of these catalysts is significantly related to their nanoparticle sizes [13, 14, 17], morphologies [15, 18, 19], crystal orientations[20] and oxidation states [16]. In recent reports, Zhu et al. have demonstrated the variation in activities of size-controlled monodisperse Au nanoparticles for electrochemical CO2 reduction in an aqueous 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte [14]. They have reported that Au nanoparticles with a size of 8 nm showed the highest CO faradaic efficiency (FE) of ~90% at -0.67 VRHE. A computational study tries to explain this catalytic performance of Au nanoparticles based on the presence of an edge site, which promotes the adsorption and stabilization of a key intermediate COOH*, which exists on 8 nm Au nanoparticles at an optimum level [14]. For Ag electrocatalysts, Lu and his colleagues have recently reported the morphological effect of Ag on electrochemical CO production [18]. At - 0.50 VRHE, the CO FE values with various morphologies of Ag catalysts have been recorded as ~90 % for nanoporous Ag, ~40 % for an Ag nanoparticle, negligible for polycrystalline Ag and negligible for an Ag nanowire. In addition, the nanoporous Ag showed good stability maintaining its CO FE for 8 hours. However, these noble metal electrocatalysts are expensive,
5
which is one of the main hurdles for their commercialization.
Cu is one of the most cost-effective electrocatalysts for electrochemical CO2 reduction [21- 27], and the activity and selectivity of Cu electrocatalysts are known to be related to the size of the nanoparticles [21], morphologies [22, 23], crystal orientations [24-26] and oxidation states [27]. When Cu is used as an alloy or an overlayer with Au and Ag, its catalytic performance for CO production is enhanced and modified at lower costs [28-32]. Kim et al. prepared Au-Cu bimetallic nanoparticles by co-reducing the gold and copper precursors using a one-pot synthesis method [28]. With the Au-Cu bimetallic nanoparticles as catalysts, various products were obtained in the electrochemical reduction of CO2 and their CO FE was dependent on the Au/Cu ratio. The Au3Cu catalyst exhibited a better turnover rate (TOR) than pure Au, which can be explained by the fact that Au-Cu bimetallic nanoparticles have a Cu atom near the Au-C primary bond, which can bind the O atom of COOH, so that the stabilization of COOH is easier. Additionally, Au-Cu nanoparticles also showed better mass activity.
In the present study, our strategy to enhance CO production with an emphasis on costeffectiveness, focuses on the preparation of Ag-Cu dendritic structures using electrodeposition. Electrodeposition has some advantages over the conventional catalyst synthesis methods; it’s a very simple and cheap process enabling easy control of composition and shape of the catalysts. Under controlled deposition potentials and electrolyte composition, our simple electrodeposition
6
method facilitates morphological and compositional control of Ag-Cu dendrites providing a large surface area for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO. A careful examination of the material properties of Ag-Cu dendrites revealed that a synergetic effect between Ag and Cu exists in these catalysts, which may play a role in cost-effectiveness for practical applications.
7

sections.heading: 2. Experimental
sections.text:
2.1. Preparation of Ag-Cu catalysts
The catalysts were prepared on a Cu foil substrate using an electrodeposition method. KAg(CN)2 and CuCN were used as the Ag and Cu precursors, respectively, for electrodeposition, with KCN playing the role of a complexing agent. The concentrations of KCN and CuCN were fixed at 0.4 M and 0.2 M, respectively, while various concentrations of KAg(CN)2 from 10 mM to 30 mM were used in order to vary the composition ratios of Ag and Cu. Pure Ag and pure Cu electrodes were also prepared as controls. 0.5 M KCN and 0.1 M KAg(CN)2 were used for the deposition of pure Ag, while 0.2 M KCN and 0.1 M CuCN were used for the deposition of pure Cu.
Electrodeposition and linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) were conducted in a three-electrode cell system. Cu foil loaded into a Teflon holder with a fixed exposure area of 7.1 cm2 was used as the working electrode. The area of the working electrode, the charge consumed during the deposition and the EDS analysis results were used for calculating the Ag loading mass. A silver reference electrode (Ag/AgCl(sat. KCl)) was used in our three-electrode system. For the counter electrodes, Ag wire was used for the deposition of Ag-Cu and pure Ag, while Cu wire was used for the deposition of pure Cu. Electrodeposition was conducted using a potentiostat (EG&G 273A, Princeton Applied Research). The deposition potentials were chosen through LSV
8
experiments. Initially, LSV for selecting the deposition potential was conducted in the abovementioned electrolytes across a potential range from -0.4 V to -2.0 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) at a sweep rate of 20 mV/s. Ag-Cu electrodes were deposited from the electrolyte containing both Ag and Cu precursors at -1.3 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) using a fixed amount of charge (400 mC/cm2) passing through. Ag catalyst was prepared by a two-step electrodeposition to cover the Cu substrate completely and form a layer with a large surface area. Ag layer of high surface coverage was formed at -0.7 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) for 100 mC/cm2 charge passed and then further Ag was formed at -1.8 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) for 400 mC/cm2 of charge. Dendritic Cu was formed at -2.0 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) for a higher amount of charge (3 C/cm2) passing through owing to the competing evolution of hydrogen.
2.2 The characterization of Ag, Ag-Cu and Cu electrodes The electrodeposited Ag-Cu catalysts were characterized by field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM; S-4800, Hitachi) and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS; INCA Energy, Oxford Instruments Analytical Ltd.) to investigate the morphology of the surface and the bulk composition, respectively. The surface composition of each Ag-Cu catalyst was investigated by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS; AXIS-HSi, KRATOS) and highresolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM; JEM-3010, Jeol). The crystalline
9
structure of the materials was analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD; D8-Advance, BRUKER).
2.3. Electrochemical CO2 reduction to CO Electrochemical reduction of CO2 was performed in an H-type cell(batch type) made of poly carbonate, and all experiments were performed at room temperature and ambient pressure [33]. The cathodic part and the anodic part were separated by Nafion® NRE-212. All the experiments were carried out in a three-electrode cell system. Fabricated catalysts (Ag, Ag-Cu, Cu) were used as the working electrodes with a geometrical area of 4.9 cm2. SCE was used as the reference electrode with Pt gauze functioning as the counter electrode. An aqueous solution of KHCO3 (0.5 M) was used as both catholyte and anolyte in the experiments. The electrolytes were purged with N2 gas for at least 30 minutes. After that, the catholyte was saturated with CO2 gas under a flow rate of 300 mL/min for at least 45 minutes. Electrochemical reduction potential of CO2 was first investigated by performing LSV from 0 V to -2.0 V (vs. SCE) at a sweep rate of 50 mV/s. The reduction potential range was determined by comparing the reduction current of the LSV experiment in each catholyte (CO2-free or CO2-saturated). Subsequently, chronoamperometry for CO2 reduction was performed for 30 minutes at -1.3 V, -1.5 V, -1.7 V and -1.9 V (vs. SCE). The catalytic activity was measured using the reduction current during the experiment in each solution and the concentration of produced CO and H2. A potentiostat
10
(Wavenow, Pine Instruments) was used for all the electrochemical CO2 reduction experiments. CO and H2 produced at the surface of the working electrode were directly delivered to the sampling loop of a gas chromatography system (Agilent 7890A) in real-time through a line at the top of the cathodic compartment. CO2 gas was continuously bubbled into the catholyte at a constant rate of 10 sccm controlled by a mass flow controller (MFC; MKS Instruments Inc.), which was also used for delivering the gaseous products directly into the gas chromatography system. The gas chromatography system consisted of both a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and a flame ionization detector (FID) with methanizer, which were used to analyze H2 and CO, respectively. The concentrations of detected CO and H2 were compared with the charge consumed for CO2 reduction so that it can be used for calculating the faradaic efficiency.
11

sections.heading: 3. Results and Discussion
sections.text:
Figure 1 demonstrates the LSV analysis of Ag and Cu electrolytes on the Cu foil substrate. In order to fabricate the Ag-Cu deposits with various compositions, the concentration of Ag(CN)2 in the electrolytes was varied from 10 to 30 mM at a fixed CuCN concentration (0.2 M). For both the LSV analysis and electrodeposition, an Ag/AgCl (sat. KCl) electrode was used as the reference electrode. Three clear reduction regions were observed in the LSV plots for all the electrolytes as marked in Figure 1 (region I, II and III). As the concentration of Ag ions increased, the reduction current starting at approximately -0.40 V gradually increased, indicating that the region I can be attributed to Ag ion reduction on the Cu foil substrate. With the more negative sweep passing the peak potential at -0.67 V, the Ag deposition process was controlled by mass transfer limitation. The increase in reduction current in the range of -1.00 ~ - 1.10 V was not significantly affected by the concentration of Ag ion. This could mean that Cu ion reduction was now occurring on the Ag deposit/Cu foil substrate in the region II. Further current increase observed in region III could correspond to a proton reduction reaction on the Ag-Cu deposits/Cu foil substrate leading to hydrogen evolution. More information on CN-based electrolyte is available in our previous work [34].
Figure 2 shows the FESEM images of Ag, Ag-Cu and Cu catalysts electrodeposited at constant potentials. For Ag100, high surface coverage was required to eliminate the underlying
12
Cu substrate effect. Hence, the deposition was initially performed at a moderate potential of -0.7 V for high coverage and then at -1.8 V for obtaining a high surface area structure. Hierarchical dendritic structures of Ag-Cu were fabricated at -1.3V where the deposition was dominated by mass transport. The nomenclatures of Ag-Cu catalysts were determined from their bulk compositions, which were analyzed by EDS. Figure 2(a) shows the morphology of pure Ag deposited by the two-step deposition as described in the experimental section. As shown in the enlarged image, relatively round shaped multi-pod structures were formed with the size range of 300 ~ 400 nm. It is noted that the formation of well-defined Ag multi-pod structures originated at low concentrations of Ag precursor used, which enabled mass transfer limited growth. Similarly, the Ag-Cu hierarchical structure was formed at a negative deposition potential of -1.3 V and low concentration of Ag ions as confirmed by LSV analysis. However, the structure of Ag-Cu catalysts showed drastic changes to the dendrites. At a small Cu composition of 16 %, the formation of flower-like shape with long and sharp branches was observed as presented in Figure 2(b). When the Cu composition increased from 16 % to 43 % the branches became relatively small along with an increase in the number density of the branches. Similar formations of dendritic structure have been reported previously. Zhou et al. prepared an Ag dendrite by lowering the concentration of an Ag nitrate solution so that the process was under mass transfer limitation [35], while Eom et al. confirmed that the formation of a Ni-Ag alloy
13
dendrite occurred in low concentrations of Ag nitrate solution by controlling the current density [36]. However, for the Ag-Cu deposition reported in this work, it seems that the dendritic structures were also affected by the unique structures of both pure Ag and Cu. Meanwhile, a continuous film with its surface terminated by numerous prominences was observed in the FESEM image of pure Cu deposited at -2.0 V as shown in Figure 2(e).
The electrodeposited Ag, Ag-Cu and Cu were analyzed by XRD to investigate the crystalline structure and the XRD data is shown in Figure 3. For Ag100 sample, the peak positions of Ag(111), Ag(200), Ag(220) and Ag(311) are located at 38.2°, 44.3°, 64.5° and 77.4°, respectively [37]. This indicates that the electrodeposited Ag dendrite exists as polycrystalline Ag. The Cu (111) at 43.4°, (200) at 50.5°, and (220) at 74.2° in the Ag100 sample were from the Cu substrate. When the Cu content is increased in the Ag-Cu catalysts all the peak intensities of Ag decreased while the Cu crystalline peaks of Cu (111), (200), and (220) from both Cu substrate and dendrite Cu were maintained. The significant decrease in Ag peaks by the addition of Cu in the deposits implies that the co-deposited Cu inhibited the crystal growth of Ag, which might be one of the reasons for the dramatic changes in the morphologies observed from Ag100 to AgxCuy samples as shown in figure 2. Additionally, there is no shift in the peak positions of both Cu and Ag thereby indicating that there are no changes to the lattice parameter. Therefore, the condition used in the present experiment has a dominant effect on the control of the structure,
14
not on the formation of alloy.
LSV analysis was performed on the electrodeposited Ag, Ag-Cu and Cu catalysts in 0.5 M KHCO3 with N2 and CO2 purging in order to investigate the potential range in which the CO2 reduction reaction would occur. The results of these experiments are shown in Figure 4. In the N2-purged electrolyte (dashed line), the onset potential of the cathodic reaction on Ag100 catalyst was observed at approximately -1.2 VSCE (Figure 4a). Most of the reduction current contributed to the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) on the Ag100 catalyst. However, in the CO2 purged electrolyte (solid line), the onset potential was slightly shifted to the positive range, indicating that the CO2 reduction was occurring. The onset potential of HER on Cu100 catalyst in the N2purged electrolyte was similar to that of Ag100 catalyst, but the current increased rapidly with a negative potential sweep, showing better activity of Cu for HER. On the other hand, in the case of CO2-purged electrolyte, Ag100 catalysts exhibited higher reduction currents in all potential ranges negative to the onset potential. The difference in the currents between N2-purged and CO2-purged electrolytes indicated that the CO2 reduction occurred simultaneously with HER. However, in the case of the Cu100 catalyst, the overall profile of the i-v curve in CO2-purged electrolyte was similar to that in the N2-purged case. A slight increase in the current compared to the N2-purged case was observed in the potential range between -1.20 and 1.38V (box figure). As the potential was shifted to a more negative value to -2.0V, a very tiny increase in the current
15
was re-occurring. This indicates that the CO2 reduction on Cu in the electrolyte used in this work is not very efficient and may generate different reduction products at different potential regions. The reduction peak in the potential range between -0.35 to -0.60 V corresponds to the reduction of Cu oxides [23]. Figure 4b-d demonstrates the potentiodynamic differences between N2-purged and CO2-purged electrolytes on various Ag-Cu dendrite catalysts. Firstly, all of the samples show that the current increases with CO2-purged electrolyte close to the onset potentials. It should be noted that the reduction currents for all Ag-Cu dendrites increase more rapidly after the onset potentials compared to the Ag100 or Cu100 catalysts. This is probably due to the hierarchical structures of Ag-Cu dendrites resulting in larger surface areas. As the Cu content in the catalyst increases (figure 4b to 4d), the differences in the current densities between N2purged and CO2-purged electrolytes decreased (box figures in Figure 4b to 4d) indicating that the CO2 reduction on Ag-Cu dendrites were mostly done by Ag. Considering this inference along with Figure 2 and 3, it can be concluded that Cu contents in Ag-Cu dendrites contribute only to the control of the shape or morphology of the catalyst and CO2 reduction was occurring mostly on Ag present in the Ag-Cu dendrite catalysts. Additionally, the copper oxide reduction peaks gradually increased as the Cu contents increased.
From the LSV analysis, several potentials were selected to reduce the CO2 on Ag, Ag-Cu and Cu catalysts for 30 minutes. Faradaic efficiency (FE) for CO and H2were calculated by using the
16
total reduction charge and produced gas concentration as shown in Figure 5. In the case of the Cu100 dendrite catalyst, the FE for CO (< 6.0 %) is very low at all potentials which is similar to previous reports [38], where the HER was dominant (> 74.1 %). Notably, 6.0% FE of Cu100 at - 1.3V, the highest CO FE in the case of Cu, is in good accordance with the noticeable difference in CO2 reduction currents between N2-purged and CO2-purged electrolytes on Cu100 at -1.3V in Figure 4a (box figure). The rest of FE for Cu100 at -1.3, -1.5, and -1.7 V is associated with other products such as methane [39]. For the Ag100 catalyst, FE for CO production was 17.9 % at -1.3 VSCE and the highest value of 64.6 % was achieved when the potential was held at -1.7 VSCE. At a highly negative potential of -1.9 VSCE, the FE for CO decreased to 36.5 %. On the other hand, the FE for H2 was 28.6 % at -1.3 VSCE, and it decreased to 13.5 % even as the potential was shifted to a negative value (-1.9 VSCE) as shown in Figure 5b. This indicates that the reduction of CO2 to CO is most efficient at -1.5 to -1.7 V while HER or conversion of CO2 to other products dominated at either higher or lower potential ranges, an inference which is in good accordance with Figure 4a. From a comparison with other catalysts, the Ag100 catalyst shows higher CO FE at all potentials except at -1.3 VSCE. Interestingly, the synergetic effects of Ag-Cu dendrite catalyst on CO FE were observed at -1.3 VSCE, however it vanished when the potential was moved into the negative range. The Ag84Cu16 dendrite catalyst demonstrates a CO FE of 43.9 % at -1.3 VSCE, which is 2.5 times larger than in the Ag100 case. At the same potential, a small
17
increase in CO FE for Ag75Cu25 and Ag57Cu43catalysts were observed compared to the Ag100 catalyst. Overall, CO FE has a tendency to decrease with an increase in the Cu content due to the increasing H2 FE in the case of the Ag-Cu dendrites.
Figure 6 exhibits the CO mass activity obtained by CO FE with respect to the Ag mass loading that has been calculated from charges consumed during the Ag-Cu electrodeposition and the EDS analysis results. The calculated Ag loading masses were 3.95 mg for Ag100, 2.38 mg for Ag84Cu16, 1.90 mg for Ag75Cu25 and 1.26 mg for Ag57Cu43, respectively. Among all catalysts, the CO mass activity achieves the highest value of 30.5 %/mgAg with the Ag57Cu43 catalyst at -1.5 VSCE whereas the Ag100 catalyst shows its highest value of 16.3 %/mgAg at -1.7 VSCE. It should be noted that all of the Ag-Cu catalysts demonstrate higher CO mass activities than the Ag100 catalyst at the potentials of -1.3 and -1.5 VSCE. However, at more negative potentials of -1.7 and -1.9V, the CO mass activity of Ag-Cu catalysts were similar or slightly lower than that of the Ag100 catalyst, owing to the higher HER activity of Ag-Cu as shown in Figure 5b. From the above discussion, it can be concluded that the Ag-Cu dendrite catalyst can be used as an efficient catalyst for electrochemical CO formation from CO2 at relatively low reduction potentials with less Ag usage.
Further, the surface compositions of the catalysts were analyzed by XPS as shown in Figure 7. The Cu surface composition was plotted as a function of Ag ion concentration in the
18
electrolytes for electrodeposition. In all the samples, the amount of Cu at the surface of the AgCu dendrite catalysts is higher than that in bulk as measured by EDS, which conceivably indicates that Cu segregation is carried out from the catalyst bulk. It is well known that Ag and Cu are mostly immiscible with each other due to their significant lattice mismatch. However, several immiscible elements form two-dimensional alloys at the surface [40], including Ag-Cu as reported by Linic et al.[41]. Although the surface energy of Ag(111) (γAg(111) = 0.078 eV/Å2 [42]) is much lower than that of Cu (γCu(111) = 0.114 eV/Å2 [43]), it has been reported that Cu segregates to the surface in the presence of minimum of 0.25 monolayer of oxygen [44]. A strong affinity of Cu towards oxygen facilitates Cu segregation overcoming the unfavorable surface energy effect. The adsorption energy with 0.25 monolayer of oxygen coverage on Ag(111) is 0.38 eV/atom, while on Cu(11) it is 1.57 eV/atom [44]. Therefore, based on literature, we infer that the Cu segregates on the surface of fabricated Ag-Cu dendrite catalysts in the presence of oxygen in the air. The compositional difference between surface and bulk Cu was in the range from 12.9 % to 17.9 %. The trend in the compositional difference between surface and bulk is not very easy to explain, but is thought to be related to the difference in the morphologies of the Ag-Cu catalyst. Different Ag compositions may have different effects on contact with oxygen. In addition, small experimental errors might exist in the measurement of Cu surface content by XPS because of the underlying Cu foil substrate, which could affect the
19
compositional analysis, even though similar error would be present in the EDS measurements.
For the confirmation of the Cu-rich surface structure, a sample catalyst with the lowest Cu contents (Ag84Cu16) was further analyzed with TEM and the results are shown in Figure 8. Several sub-branches were observed at the surface of the main branches (Figure 8a). In the enlarged image (Figure 8b), the surface of the sub-branches shows the boundaries which could be distinguished by a large difference in contrast and electron diffraction (inset images). In order to confirm this, we measured the elemental maps of a branch of Ag84Cu16 dendrite catalyst (partial collapse of hierarchical dendrite structure was found during TEM analysis at high voltage) as shown in Figure 8c-f. The Ag and Cu were uniformly distributed in the dendrite structure, and it was found that surface Cu concentration was relatively high in spite of its low concentration in bulk (Ag84Cu16). This inference is also supported by elemental line scanning as illustrated in Figure 8g. All these results together reasonably support the Cu-rich surface as has been indicated in Figure 7. This is also the reason that the Ag-Cu catalyst showed a lower selectivity than Ag100 for the CO2 reduction to CO. Hence, catalysts with this structure can be applied effectively to the direct production of syngas (mixture of CO and H2) by controlling the Cu content. For instance, in case of Ag75Cu25 catalyst from Figure 5, product composition at -1.7 VSCE was approximately H2:CO=2:1, which can be applied to direct syngas production from CO2 reduction. Likewise, the Cu-rich surface also leaves room for further investigation on the
20
effect of surface Cu contents on the CO FE and gas composition. Modification of surface Cu contents, for example by annealing or etching, may further affect the product gas composition or the mass activity to CO production.
In summary, we have fabricated hierarchical Ag-Cu dendrite catalysts by electrodeposition for application as catalysts for the reduction of CO2 to CO. Though FE for CO production was highest for the Ag100 catalyst, more then 2-times increase in the mass activity (with respect to Ag) was obtained for our Ag-Cu dendrite catalysts. Cu in the Ag-Cu catalysts play a significant role in the control of morphology, and segregates to the surface of the dendrite. By controlling the composition of Ag and Cu, direct formation of syn-gas or enhancement in the mass activity to CO production was achievable.
21

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In the present research, we fabricated Ag-Cu catalysts by an electrodeposition method and analyzed their activities towards electrochemical CO2 reduction. The surface structure and the composition of Ag-Cu catalysts were controlled by changing the concentration of precursors in the electrolyte. For Ag-Cu catalysts, it was found that they have hierarchical dendritic structures, while pure Ag has a multi-pod structure and pure Cu has a film-like structure with a prominences-terminated surface. Electrochemical CO2 reduction was performed at several potentials to investigate the activity of the Ag-Cu dendrite catalysts. Though pure Ag has the highest CO FE at relatively high reduction potential of -1.7V, Ag mass-normalized FE (mass activity) was highest in the case of Ag57Cu43 at -1.5V. This implies that Ag-Cu dendritic catalysts can be effectively applied to CO production by electrochemical CO2 reduction. These catalysts present great advantages in terms of process costs (in both terms of catalyst cost and input energy). It was also found that the surface of Ag-Cu catalyst was enriched with Cu due to the segregation of Cu.
22

sections.heading: Highlights
sections.text: Ag-Cu dendrite catalysts are fabricated for electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO. The mass activity of Ag57Cu43 catalyst is 2.2 times higher than that of Ag catalyst. The composition of produced gas (H2 + CO) is a strong function of Ag:Cu ratio.
